items.body:
Stefan Betke aka Pole’s hugely influential debut LP of frayed dub experiments resurfaces for a 20th anniversary reissue, taking us back to smoked out nights at the turn of the century and some of the finest post basic-channel dub echoes ever released. Essential listening if you’re into anything from Rhythm & Sound to Vainqueur, Jon Hassell to Jackie Mittoo.

As legend goes, Pole took his name from a malfunctioning Waldorf 4-Pole filter which produced hisses and pops which weren’t really controllable or predictable, much like a living organism. Betke realised the potential and came to alchemically morph and render them with judicious FX dubbing into a groundbreaking sort of minimalist electro-dub that sounds exceedingly good with a spliff and glass of booze. Working somewhere between the variants of abstract techno on Chain Reaction and Mille Plateaux’s cutting edge minimalist strains, Pole’s first trio of albums inarguably helped lay the foundations for dub techno as it’s come to be known and are held in the highest regard by practically everyone who owns them. 

The Pole aesthetic is patently laid out in ‘1’, where his organic clicks ’n pops come out to play accompanied by lilting organ and jazzy bass channelling Jackie Mittoo via Jon Hassell and Rhythm & Sound into a uniquely, gauzy, gaseous state.  So strong was the impact of the album on the late ‘90s underground, they even generated a “pastiche” that was unwittingly issued (and subsequently deleted) by Fat Cat on their split series, but was purportedly made by V/Vm in a snidey but frankly hilarious prank, albeit one that demonstrates just how ubiquitous and influential Betke’s sound was at the time. More than that, it’s fair to say the 20 year cycle hasn’t rinsed out the appeal of this triptych one bit; it remains one of electronic music’s most enigmatic and strangely moving, tactile bodies of work.

All upward lift and kosmiche synth iridescence from Seoul’s blissed family band, back on the Far East’s leading krautrock revival label, Guruguru Brain...

“The blissed family band is back! TENGGER have always moved together, through time, space & genre. 'SKY' arrives as a new chapter: a little more still, a little more inward, while keeping all the warmth that's always been at the heart of what they do.

Embodying the band name meaning "endless sky" in Mongolian and "vast sea" in Hungarian, their 8th album 'SKY' centres on the feelings of boundless, infinite expansion. Conceived as one continuous environment rather than a collection of tracks, the album unfolds slowly through luminous synths, patient drones and Itta's breath-like vocals.

Like a soft big sky you can actually float on: 'SKY' is vast, warm, and wide open.

"Rather than a specific emotion, we hope the record opens a certain awareness — that the sky is not just something to be seen. Through it, we sense a connection to something much larger — a feeling of being linked to the wider universe. This sense of connection runs through the entire record.””

items.body:
Reissue of the debut by A.G. Cook & Danny L Harle’s earliest duo, Dux Content, initially dispensed on Gamsonite, a predecessor of P.C. Music, and teasing out strands of makina, electro-house, bardcore and trap with combo’s of ludic, recombinant suss & sharp sound design that became their calling card.

Scrolling back to what now feels like a distant world - the up-for-grabs edges of early 2010s - ‘Lifestyle’ maps out formative aspects of the two producers, still relatively fresh from music studies at Goldsmiths, and making their mark in a burgeoning “internet music” scene. Of course they’re both now chart-topping songwriters/producers with credits for Charli xcx, Dua Lipa, Oklou, et al, but here they’re positively bubbling over with wild, yet disciplined, fusions of upfront hard dance with jazz, contemporary classical and pop that, with the benefit of hindsight, place them in a contemporaneous cultural slipstream with likes of Cracksmurf/T C F or James Ferraro, and soon-to-be spar, SOPHIE.

‘Lifestyle’ is the sound of two minds scything thru cultures and sounds they grew up with - Harle coming from a family background spanning his Geordie dad, John Harle’s BBC scores and early taste for makina’s stacked melodies - and bonding over a shared love of Captain Beefheart, Archie Sheep, and Tim & Eric, all evident in their grasp of shiny, commercial hooks and complex rhythm wrapped up with daft grin and wink. Shake a wand anywhere and you’ll hit a mad one, from the crazed midi piano house of ‘Voice of an Angel’, thru the jazz-fink of ‘City Break’ and ‘Hero Next Door’, free wheeling jazz trance of ‘Heart of Death’ and pitch bent panpipes of ‘Business Class’.

Picking up where 2024's 'Trash Can Lamb' left off, Keith Freund blurs the line between acoustic instrumentation and DIY electronics on his latest full-length, unraveling his gentle, jazzy sessions with 8-bit beats and oddball FX.

Since the beginning, Freund has been fixated on the character of a sound rather than what that sound, on its own, might represent. His piano parts rarely come off as if they've been played by hand; after chopping them to shreds, he inevitably reconstitutes them into player-piano style impossible sequences, re-organizing the notes and re-sculpting the tone completely. On 'Over Sidewalk Bryum', for example, it's the piano that provides the track's rhythm, accented by radio interference and bit-crushed oscillations. And although Freund does less chipping at his horn parts, letting the sax soar over the chattering electronics, it's still subtly tweaked - nothing's ever quite what it seems.

A swamp of discarded blips and glitches help prop up 'I'll Find a Place for Us', and Freund's soft woodwind tones make their way through the noise initially - or at least that's what we're supposed to think. In time, Freund's sax emerges and the soft-hued, woodwind-like sound is revealed to be a red herring. But that's the kind of sleight of hand that Freund seems to revel in, creating glitchy, unstable music from soft, placid sound sources, not the harsh digital detritus you'd expect to find on a Mille Plateaux disc.

items.body:
Moving sideways from Warp to Domino, Simian Mobile Disco's James Ellis Ford challenges himself on his second solo full-length, crafting a set of Sakamoto-inspired synth pop from his hospital bed.

Ford's always been capable of producing pitch-perfect pop - his appearance on records from everyone from the Pet Shop Boys to Depeche Mode is a testament to that - but 'Lost in Another World' is a more personal affair. It was written and produced in hospital after he'd been diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia last year, "on the ward between rounds of chemo." Thankfully his condition has improved - he posted earlier this month that he's got no more treatment in store - but the album stands as a vulnerable reflection of a difficult time. Ford describes it as a "pep talk", and it draws on some of his most enduring influences, Yellow Magic Orchestra and Japan, to channel its complicated tangle of emotions. 

On the opening track (and lead single) 'Overtones', Ford's voice hovers over plasticky rhythmelodic sequences and rubbery '80s drums and you'd be forgiven for assuming it's a lost city pop demo. Ford doesn't let the energy fall off, either, waltzing through slow-motion melancholia on the tentatively beautiful 'Here Today' and John Foxx-style synth pop on 'This Too Shall Pass'. Ultimately, it's surprisingly hopeful material, infused with genuine feeling.

Recorded live in Brooklyn, 'Somewhere in the Wind' is Loren Connors & David Grubbs’ third album and their first as a guitar duo, showcasing their free-er, noiser side with two extended, ecstatic jams. 

Thankfully, we didn't have to wait another two decades to hear Grubbs and Connors collide again. Their first album, 'Arborvitae', appeared way back in 2003, not long after the duo had first met when Connors shared a bill with Gastr del Sol. But it wasn't until 2024 that they rekindled that magic, shaking things up a little and swapping roles on keys and guitar, with Connors even moonlighting on drums. 'Somewhere in the Wind' might be the perfect companion to that record, recorded last year at Blank Forms, it's their first session featuring both players on electric guitar and it's a joy to engage with on every level. Both distinctive players carry an unmistakable signature style, complementing each other by leaning into the noise and freedom of their collaboration in a way we hadn't witnessed until now. 

If their first two records dug into crepuscular space, the domain of Roy Montgomery and Harold Budd, this one takes its cues from the physicality of their instruments and the knowledge they've acquired along the way. You feel as if you're practically in the room with them as Connors's blurry post-blues recitals casually interact with Grubbs' obsessively tuned intonations. On the first side, we walk into what might as well be a prayer, each note played in reverence to something or someone. But as the piece accumulates weight, so too do the notes, lovingly distorted and pushed off track until all that's left is raw emotion. On the flip, the duo sound even more possessed, kicking up the energy so the notes bounce around the very edges of the recording space. It's a document of two players who don't have anything left to prove.

items.body:
Scoring a graphic novel based on a dream he had in 2024, John Carpenter gets the band back together, turning in an album that'll delight fans of 'Lost Themes'.

We know full well that Hollywood doesn't seem interested in making Carpenter's films a reality any more - he's said as much, quite publicly. So what's the next best thing? Well, a graphic novel. 'Cathedral' was written by Carpenter alongside his wife (and long-time creative partner) Sandy King and, like all great Carpenter projects, it had to have a home-brewed score to ease it along. So who better to make the dream a reality than his regular bandmates Cody Carpenter and Daniel Davies? Chronologically, this one fits in right after 2024's 'Lost Themes No. 4: Noir', but fans of Carpenter's earlier (eerier) biz will be happy to hear that he's reaching a little further back this time. 

There's of course the hard rock influence that's been present since at least 'They Live', but every so often there's a glimmer of the earworm-laden synth pop that elevated 'Escape from New York', and the iconic 'Assault on Precinct 13'. Just peep the 'Halloween'-style piano breakdown on 'Inside Out', the 'In the Mouth of Madness' mood on opener 'Primeval' or the classic horror flex of 'Abandoned Cathedral', with its organs, orchestral swells and all-important Mellotron choirs.

items.body:
Anyone obsessed with those two incredible ‘Begena Songs…’ comps on Death Is Not The End will be properly enchanted by this more expansive - yet still intimate - suite of snapshots from Ethiopia, 1971, spanning the unique, twanging harp sound thru to Amharic poetry, chants, and spellbinding flute dances...

One that catches the breath with seldom felt sensations, ‘Ethiopian Musics 1971’ patently owes as much to the incredible performers as their faithful representation in Ragnar Johnson & Ralph Harrisson’s recordings. All secreted to tape on a Uher Report L stereo reel-to-reel recorder, they epitomise an era of ethnomusicological preservation, when the likes of labels such as Lyrichord and  Folkways were already decades deep “in the field”, documenting long-held traditions practically untouched by an encroaching, western modernity. And perhaps most crucially, the recordings beautifully render the acoustic settings and vivid vibes with an immersive quality in stark opposition to the era of dry, so-called audiophile studio recordings of ethnic musics to come - all the better for immersing in this wonderfully unfamiliar world.

The abundance of singular tones and strong, rare feels they produce is quite staggering to our northern english ears, and we reckon also for anyone else, for that matter. Opening to a joyful couplet of a bluesy ’Song about the beauty of women’, and the almost shanty-like swing and hard rhythm of ’Tej Beit Song’, the set reels to distinctive pieces of Ethiopian Christian song set to begena, or ‘Harp of David’, buzz, and a landscape-scale, 13 minute ‘Love Song (Mary Armede)’. A gripping ‘Drum Song (Jigsaw)’ will be mana to rhythm fiends, and a number of standout flute pieces reprise the frisson of our first encounter with this discipline on Sublime Freq’s ‘Staring into the Sun - Ethiopian Tribal Music’ set of 2012, most potently on the pluming twin pipes of the ‘Fila Flute Dance’ parts, whilst the pentatonic craar (6-stringed lyre) parts surely strike nerves for lovers of the rawest blues, and hail the liberated legacy of Mary Armede, a folk singer-fashion designer of Azmari heritage who surely warrants further investigation. 

No doubt this is one of the most striking archival discoveries of 2026, acutely advised to anyone enchanted with music from this corner of the world from Éthiopiques to begena harp, thru to Ragnar Johnson’s other arenas of research for Ideologic Organ in Yemen or Papua New Guinea. Dive in without delay.

items.body:
Thee darkest, weirdest dub perennial from Keith Hudson, 1979, blooms on vinyl for first time in years, ready to scatter smoke and minds into the late and early hours...

First released in 1979 and highly in-demand ever since, the dub sibling to Keith Hudson’s ‘Nuh Skin Up’ pushes that album’s already stark blooz and The Soul Syndicate’s deadly riddims hard into the echo chamber with a balance of experimental nous and heads-down grooves that has assured its place in the pantheon of the most haunting dubs. 

Out of print for decades until a 2007 pressing spiked it back in the water table, the album firmly holds up nearly a half century since its original release on the basis of a future proofed minimalism that continues to haunt successive generations with its bony percussion and a dematerialised soul exemplary of dub metaphysics at its transcendant best.

Up there with the likes of Lee ‘Scratch’ Perry in terms of his dual role as songwriter and desk-tweaking dub maverick, Hudson really gets inside his own tunes, and The Soul Syndicate’s instrumentals, with the uncanniest insight, turning the likes of its title corker into clouds of pillowy steppers bass and streaking echoic contrails.

The way he inverts the vocals on ‘Ire Ire’ to sound properly wrong-end-of-telescope against the foregrounded crack of congas and spectral organ is just magic, and lays the groundwork for so much dub experimentation to come from the likes of everyone from Rhythm & Sound to Tricky, along with the likes of his spellbinding, skeletal steppers dub masterwork ‘Troubles’.

items.body:
Mu-inspired space cadets KiF Productions livicate their play of Japanese environmental ambient electronics, Hassellian 4th world, the KLF’s ‘Chill Out’, and Eno-esque harmonic perfumes, to the dearly departed Keith McIvor​.

"Passiflora (Passifloraceae) is a genus of around 550 species of flowering plants, native to the tropical and subtropical Americas. The Passion Flower is a plant of improbable beauty - its blooms almost too intricate to be real, its climbing habit a quiet kind of determination. It has been used for centuries as a remedy for anxiety and sleeplessness, something that slows us and the world around us down.

Fresh from last year's triumphant debut by KiF; Still Out, Passiflora, the album, follows the plant from its very beginning. It opens in darkness - 'Secret of the Seed', dormant, waiting - before the first tentative stir of 'First Movement' and the long, instinctive reach of 'Seeking Light'. From there, the journey unfolds with the patience of something that has no choice but to grow: drinking, climbing, flowering. 'Song of the Vine' carries the plant's quiet insistence upward, while 'Florescence' and 'Pollination Dream' catch it at its most open - that brief, extraordinary moment of full bloom. Then the turn. 'Fruiting (Slight Return)' and finally 'Return to Earth' - the cycle completing itself, giving back what it always borrowed.

Each track is a stage. The whole is a life cycle."

items.body:
Roping in Pierre Bastien and Mark Cunningham to provide brass, Mike Cooper turns in his most kaleidoscopic fourth world dream sequence to date, drawing on dub and exotica to harmonise with Andrew Pekler's marooned soundscapes...

Cooper admits in the liner notes that although he's often compared with Jon Hassell, it's German painter Mati Klarwein fantastical album covers that always reminded him exactly why he was doing what he was doing. Because Cooper makes music for imaginary places, not tangible soundtracks but half dreamed, half lived experiences that course through his catalog of experiments. And his process has never been quite so vivid as it is on 'Stochastic Parrot', a suite of vertiginous reverberations that are struck through with Cooper's "real and virtual" lap steel twangs, collaged together from samples and field recordings that wobble like heat haze. 

Different pockets of rhythm bash into each other on 'ARCHAEOPTERYX', accompanied by Bastien and Cunningham's spiraling brass improvisations. And Cooper holds the sounds together with his lulling repeated phrases; the hand drums might sound as if they're in conflict with the cycling drum machine crashes, but that's the point - it's not like channeling a dream so much as it's like being subjected to three or four dreams simultaneously. It's the ghosts of jazz fusion being raked over coals at midnight: just tune into 'SUMATRA SAMPHIRE', with its distant animalistic wails and popcorn drums, or the granulized 'HAT YAI', that sounds like the prelude to a druggy ritual.

items.body:
Cloud-seeding dub techno sorcery x Rhythm & Sound worship by Stephen Hitchell’s cult cv313 and Radius projects, recorded in the heart of Detroit and preserved for posterity by Pole’s faithful remasters at Scape Berlin.

Echospace co-pilot Stephen Hitchell mans the cockpit solo on six sterling examples of Motor City dub techno purism within the 1st volume of ‘Altering Illusions’. His hallucinatory, synaesthetic tekkerz are in palpable effect from the damp bass thru to its noctilucent synth haze, bathing bodies in blissed-out arrangements that unfold up to 20 minutes in length, as with the echoes of BC’s ‘radiance’ registered in expansive parting piece ‘standing still’, and dredged up from drizzly depths on the cv313 rewire of Radius’ ‘Interpolation Tapes’.

Clubs are in the rearview for an 80 min trip deep under the hood of Echospace’s classic sound, fathoming deepest levels of sunken subs and elemental attrition on ‘i s i s’, and hingeing on Rhythm & Sound’s skankers' templates in ‘hypnosphere’ and mesmerising metallic resonance of ‘irradiate’, while ‘above clouds’ rises above the weather system into clearer, blue-skied dub techno lushness; think post-storm Lake Erie panoramas diffused by Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS.

items.body:
Derek Bailey, Loren Connors and Bill Orcutt fiends will be in their element with Nathan Roche’s 2nd salvo of experimental twangers for a resurrected Celluloid; the legendary label with roots in post-punk & NYC mutations, who would also  issue ‘The Lambada’ - the biggest selling global single of ’89.

Hailing to France, via Townsville, North east Queensland, and Sydney, Australia, Nathan Roche has carved out an uncompromising catalogue of guitar abstractions since the ‘00s with myriad outfits, including turns on Siltbreeze, London’s World of Echo, and France’s excellently titled Gone With The Weed label.

After helping reboot the Celluloid label with his very psych-garage-rock LP ’35 Rue du Théâtre’ in 2025, the dozen succinct bits of ‘aa in reverse’ mark a sharp departure from the classic composure of his previous works, and into fractious deconstructions of blues guitar vernacular, very much in the vein of iconoclasts, Derek Bailey, Bill Orcutt, or Tetuzi Akiyama, but accented with his own twang.

In this abstract blues mode Nqthqn reserves the right to really jangle and pluck the listener’s nerves in tart, prickly expressions that favour microtonality and dissonance over more consonant, Western pleasures. The warp and weft of his material snags from the off with the distended notes of ‘astra’ thru the rudely detuned mix elegance and grunt in ‘aa’, pulling into Loren Connors-esue midnight melancholy on ‘aka’ and relatively stretching out into 3 mins of curdled to finely melodic chops on ‘adversary’.

Death Is Not The End return to the soul-stir sound of deep south Sacred Harp Singers in 1993 - although it could feasibly be any time since the advent of portable tape recording - in the blessed company of the Union Grove Baptist Church, Ozark, Alabama. Feels just right in this humidity…

The Wiregrass Singers' Dewey Williams began learning the shape-note tradition in his childhood. He studied under Judge Jackson, who authored the landmark 1934 hymnbook The Colored Sacred Harp. In 1971, Williams formally organized The Wiregrass Sacred Harp Singers to preserve the music full-time. This unified troupe began touring nationally and leading workshops, which ultimately launched them onto stages at the Smithsonian and Newport folk festivals up until Williams' passing in 1995 when the group disbanded. The African-American Sacred Harp tradition in the Wiregrass region has steeply declined since the start of the 21st century, due to an aging generation of singers, and today it is largely sustained through archival preservation and occasional multi-book singing meetups.

This raw recording, made at the Union Grove Baptist Church, Ozark in mid-April 1993 finds the group singing from B. F. White’s The Sacred Harp (1844), which together with his brother-in-law William Walker’s Southern Harmony (1835) formed the musical backbone of generations of Southern music and Southern musical styles.

items.body:
Colin Stetson’s breakthrough album of gripping bass sax innovations still buzzes like few others.

In 2007 ‘New History Warfare Vol.1’ asserted Stetson as an indomitable player of wind instruments, here letting off on Alto, Baritone and Bass Saxophones, plus Clarinet, in a deftly muscular display of his skills which had previously been employed on record and in live tours for Arcade Fire, Tom Waits, Bon Iver, LCD Soundsystem and whoever the heck else needed a set of lungs as good as a blacksmith’s bellows.

While perhaps best known for wielding a massive Bass Saxophone that's responsible for some of the wildest sounds on this album, Stetson proves to be a sensitive beast capable of articulating the instrument’s full range tonal in his own voice, which variously comes out resembling a purring big cat and the dying wildebeest it just stalked, attacked and slaughtered in ‘Time Is Advancing With Fitful Irregularity’, while he uses the same broad tone to describe natural scenes as textured with soil and moisture and wind as an Anne Guthrie piece in ‘As a Bird or Branch’, while ‘Nobu Take’ sounds like a manic 8-bit computer game soundtrack and ’Tiger Tiger Crane’ adds a tight percussive workout for good measure, but trust its all acoustic, instrumental, hands-on, somehow not processed. 

Still a stonking good record, this, ripe for re/discovery.
